content: Sanitary sewer overflow (SSO) refers to the release of untreated sewage into the environment, bypassing wastewater treatment systems. This phenomenon, also known as Wet Weather Overflow, is particularly relevant in developed nations with extensive sewage treatment infrastructure. The primary causes of SSO include the infiltration of excessive stormwater into sewer lines during heavy rainfall, ruptures or blockages in sewerage lines, malfunctions in pumping station lifts or power failures, and human operator errors at treatment facilities. In countries with nearly complete domestic wastewater treatment, such as the USA, Japan, the UK, and parts of Europe, an SSO event is considered a significant failure in environmental water resource management. These nations aim for comprehensive secondary treatment of all effluent and actively address deficiencies in their sewerage systems. Historically, the issue of untreated sewage discharge has been recognized since medieval times. For instance, in 16th-century England, King Henry VIII mandated that sewage troughs in London remain flowing to prevent stagnation before reaching the River Thames. However, the concept of SSO only emerged in the 19th century with the advent of wastewater treatment systems in America and parts of Europe. Initially, communities were content with having basic treatment systems and did not express significant concern about overflows until the rise of environmental awareness in the 1960s. During this period, the USA began systematically identifying SSO locations and frequencies, with the Environmental Protection Agency conducting detailed engineering analyses for major cities. The Clean Water Act of the 1980s led to billions of dollars being invested in system upgrades. By the 1990s, countries like Japan, the UK, and others in Europe began investigating their overflow issues more rigorously. The magnitude of the SSO problem is substantial. The United States government has set a goal to upgrade municipal treatment and collection systems to limit overflow events to no more than once every five years in any given community. Achieving this goal is estimated to cost approximately $88 billion, in addition to the $10 billion already invested. Although untreated sewage discharge in the USA accounts for less than 0.1% of all treated sewage, the total volume still amounts to several billion gallons annually, leading to thousands of cases of gastrointestinal illness each year. Advanced European countries and Japan report similar or slightly higher percentages of SSO events. From an engineering perspective, the most common cause of SSO is heavy rainfall, which leads to significant stormwater infiltration into sewerage lines. This issue is particularly prevalent in older cities with aging subsurface infrastructure, such as Paris, London, Stockholm, New York, and Oakland, California. Inflow into sanitary lines can result from tree root intrusion, mechanical fractures due to aging, or overpressure from vehicles and buildings above. Other system failures include power outages that disable lift station pumps or treatment plant operations, as well as mechanical breakdowns within treatment plants, such as malfunctioning trickling filter arms, clogged filters, or jammed line gates. Human error can also occasionally lead to sewage diversion and overflow events. Decentralized failures during dry weather often arise from blockages in collection sewer lines caused by debris, ruptures, or tree root intrusion. Identifying the location of such overflows is challenging due to the vast network of urban collection pipes, which can span thousands of miles, and the lack of communication between central treatment plants and individual lines unless costly monitoring equipment is installed. The human health impacts of SSO include significant numbers of gastrointestinal illnesses annually, although fatalities from single overflow events are rare. Additional consequences include beach closures, swimming restrictions, and bans on consuming certain aquatic animals, particularly mollusks, following overflow events. Ecologically, SSO can result in fish kills, harm to plankton and other aquatic microflora and microfauna, increased turbidity, and decreased dissolved oxygen levels in receiving waters. These effects exacerbate the damage caused by pathogens to aquatic ecosystems. Higher life forms, such as marine mammals, may also be affected, as certain seals and sea lions have been observed to experience peaks in pathogenic harm. Globally, the issue of SSO is difficult to contextualize, as underdeveloped countries discharge most of their sewage directly into the environment without treatment. For example, even a highly industrialized nation like China discharges approximately 55% of its sewage untreated. In Tehran, Iran, the majority of the population's sewage is injected untreated into the city's groundwater. In Venezuela, 97% of the country's sewage is discharged raw into the environment. Most of sub-Saharan Africa lacks wastewater treatment, contributing to high infant mortality rates in the region. In contrast, developed nations such as the USA, Canada, Western Europe, Australia, and Japan face a public health challenge in preventing SSO, while underdeveloped countries collectively discharge approximately 20,000 times the amount of raw sewage into the environment as these advanced nations. This equates to roughly 100 trillion gallons (380 km³) of untreated sewage annually. This stark disparity in expenditure and public health outcomes represents one of the greatest divides between developed and underdeveloped nations as of 2006.
